subject: General Knowledge
topic: Indian folk and regional paintings — mixed tiers

questions.stem: Gond painting — characterised by intricate dots, lines, and natural motifs — is a living tribal art primarily concentrated in which Indian state?

options.option_text: Chhattisgarh, known for Bastar tribal crafts and Dhokra casting
Madhya Pradesh, where the Gondi heartland includes Mandla district
Odisha, home to the Saura tribe's geometric wall-painting tradition
Jharkhand, associated with Sohrai harvest murals and Khovar art

questions.explanation: Madhya Pradesh is correct — the Gondi tribal belt centred on Mandla, Dindori, and Patangarh is the heartland of Gond painting; the late Jangarh Singh Shyam from this region placed Gond art on the national and international map. Chhattisgarh is the most tempting distractor because it also has Gondi populations and rich Bastar tribal crafts, but the canonical living Gond painting tradition is rooted in MP.

questions.stem: Kalighat pat — a 19th-century Bengali folk art known for bold outlines, flat colour washes, and satirical commentary on colonial society — originated near a famous temple in which city?

options.option_text: Puri, the pilgrimage hub closely linked to the Pattachitra scroll tradition
Kolkata, where patua artists sold scrolls near the iconic Kali temple
Varanasi, a sacred city famed for Banaras silk and ghāt-side folk arts
Vrindavan, associated with devotional Pichwai and the Braj painting school

questions.explanation: Kolkata is correct — Kalighat pat grew around the Kalighat Kali temple; local patua (scroll-painter) artists began selling simplified, vigorous paintings to pilgrims in the early 19th century. Puri is the most common distractor because it is associated with Pattachitra, a different cloth-scroll tradition from Odisha; both involve scroll-like formats but are geographically and stylistically distinct.

questions.stem: Rogan art — a GI-tagged fabric-painting technique using paint made from boiled castor oil mixed with natural pigments — survives almost exclusively in one district of Gujarat. Which district is this?

options.option_text: Vadodara, known for Pithora tribal murals of the Rathwa community
Kachchh (Kutch), where Nirona village is the sole surviving centre
Surat, Gujarat's textile capital famed for zari weaving and patola
Rajkot, associated with bandhani dyeing and traditional lacquerware

questions.explanation: Kachchh (Kutch) is correct — Rogan art is practised by the Muslim Khatri family of Nirona village in Kutch; it gained global attention when the then-US President Barack Obama received a Rogan art piece as a diplomatic gift in 2014. Vadodara is a tempting distractor because Pithora murals also belong to Gujarat's tribal belt, but Rogan is an entirely different castor-oil-based fabric technique exclusive to Kutch.

questions.stem: Pichwai paintings — large devotional cloth works mounted as liturgical backdrops behind the main idol at Nathdwara, Rajasthan — depict which deity in seasonal and festival-specific themes?

options.option_text: Rama, as depicted in the Ragamala miniature series of the Rajput school
Shrinathji, a child-form of Lord Krishna worshipped at Nathdwara shrine
Goddess Ashapura, the revered kuldevi of many Rajput and Jain clans
Hanuman, shown carrying the Dronagiri mountain in Valmiki Ramayana style

questions.explanation: Shrinathji is correct — Pichwai (literally 'behind the cloth') paintings are created exclusively for the Nathdwara temple dedicated to Shrinathji, a seven-year-old child-form of Lord Krishna depicted lifting Mount Govardhan. The paintings change with each festival and season. Rama is a plausible distractor because Rajput miniatures often depict Ramayana themes, but Pichwai is strictly a Vaishnava Krishnaite tradition centred solely on Nathdwara.

questions.stem: Both Sohrai and Khovar are wall-painting traditions of Jharkhand practised by women of the Santali, Kurmi, and Oraon communities. Sohrai is painted during harvest; for which occasion is Khovar art traditionally created?

options.option_text: Birth of a firstborn child, welcoming the new life into the household
Wedding celebrations, adorning the walls of the newly-made bridal room
Monsoon onset festivals to invoke rain deities for the coming season
Death anniversaries to invoke blessings from community ancestral spirits

questions.explanation: Wedding celebrations are correct — Khovar murals are painted on the inner walls of the bridal chamber (the word derives from 'kho' meaning hollow/cave and 'var' meaning bridegroom) to bless the new couple with fertility and prosperity. Sohrai (harvest) and Khovar (wedding) together have received GI recognition; confusing the two occasions is a very common exam error, making 'birth ceremony' a deliberately placed plausible distractor.

questions.stem: Saura paintings from the Gajapati and Koraput districts of Odisha are sometimes mistaken for Warli art due to their white-on-ochre monochromatic style. Which structural element is unique to Saura paintings and absent in Warli?

options.option_text: Warli compositions use only triangles, whereas Saura art uses only circles
The 'Idital' (sacred tree of life) forms the central axis of each Saura icon
Saura paintings are made on tanned animal hide, unlike Warli's plastered walls
Saura figures always appear in strict frontal profile, unlike Warli stick figures

questions.explanation: The 'Idital' (sacred cosmic tree / tree of life) is correct — every Saura votive painting (called an 'ikon' or 'Eksar') is structurally organised around this central tree motif, flanked by ancestral spirits (Sonum) and episodic narrative panels. Warli art, by contrast, is organised around geometric shapes depicting daily life and nature without any cosmic-tree axis. Option A is wrong because both traditions actually use multiple geometric shapes — neither restricts itself to a single form.

questions.stem: Mata ni Pachedi — a large hand-painted or block-printed cotton textile from Gujarat depicting a goddess and her court — served as a portable substitute shrine. Which marginalised community historically developed this tradition because they were denied entry into mainstream temples?

options.option_text: Rabari nomadic herders, celebrated for their distinctive mirror-work embroidery
Vaghari community, who substituted the textile for a temple they could not enter
Siddi community, descendants of East-African sailors settled along Gujarat's coast
Bharwad shepherds, renowned for woollen weaving across the Saurashtra region

questions.explanation: Vaghari community is correct — historically classified under colonial-era 'criminal tribe' legislation and denied temple access, the Vaghari community of Gujarat developed Mata ni Pachedi as a portable, home-based shrine using the textile as a sacred substitute space for goddess worship. Siddi is a tempting distractor because they are also a historically marginalised Gujarati community, but their folk traditions are rooted in African-origin music and dance, not textile shrine-making.
